sections.text: Square footage is the area of a surface in square feet, and the right formula depends on the shape: length times width for a rectangle, pi times radius squared for a circle, half base times height for a triangle. For any room that is not a single rectangle, split it into shapes you have a formula for, find each area, and add them, subtracting any part that is not floor.
Which formula goes with which shape?

rows: parallel sides 14 ft and 10 ft, 12 ft apart
base 12 ft, height 8 ft (slanted side 10 ft)
half x pi x radius squared
pi x (outer radius squared - inner radius squared)
pi x a x b (the two half-axes)
(3 x square root of 3 / 2) x side squared
2 x (1 + square root of 2) x side squared

sections.text: The Square Footage Calculator on this site handles three of these directly: rectangle, circle and L-shape. Everything else is built from those pieces by hand or from the formulas above. All values in the table were computed with a script and rounded to two decimals.
What if the room has a curved or angled part?
Treat it as a rectangle plus an extra shape. Suppose a 16 ft by 12 ft room has a semicircular bay on one wall, with the bay's straight edge the full 8 ft width of the opening, so its radius is 4 ft.

To check this in the calculator, enter the rectangle (16 by 12) to get 192, then circle mode with a radius of 4, which gives 50.27 for the full circle, and halve it. In square meters the total is 217.13 / 10.7639 = 20.17 (one square meter is about 10.7639 square feet).
How do you handle a five-sided or irregular outline?

There are two reliable methods. The first is decomposition: draw lines until you have rectangles and triangles. The second is the coordinate method (the shoelace formula): measure each corner as an x and y distance from one reference corner, then compute the area from the list of corners. Both give the same answer, which makes a good error check.

Example: a floor with corners at (0, 0), (20, 0), (20, 10), (12, 16) and (0, 12), all in feet. By decomposition, the rectangle below the line y = 10 is 20 x 10 = 200 sq ft. Above it, a triangle with a 20 ft base and 6 ft height adds 60 sq ft, and a thin triangle on the left with a 2 ft base and 12 ft height adds 12 sq ft, for 272 sq ft in total. The shoelace formula on the same five corners also gives 272. An L-shaped plan works the same way: corners (0, 0), (18, 0), (18, 8), (10, 8), (10, 14) and (0, 14) enclose 204 sq ft, matching two rectangles of 18 x 8 and 10 x 6.
How do you find the area of a triangle without the height?

If you can measure all three sides but not the height (common for an angled corner of a room), use Heron's formula. Let s be half the perimeter; the area is the square root of s x (s - a) x (s - b) x (s - c). For sides of 13, 14 and 15 ft, s = 21 and the area is the square root of 21 x 8 x 7 x 6 = 7,056, which is 84 sq ft. That agrees with the base 14, height 12 example in the table, since a 13-14-15 triangle has a 12 ft height on the 14 ft side.
What about walls and ceilings for paint?

Wall area is the room's perimeter times the ceiling height, minus openings. For a 12 ft by 15 ft room with 8 ft ceilings, the perimeter is 2 x (12 + 15) = 54 ft, so the walls are 54 x 8 = 432 sq ft. Subtract a 3 ft by 7 ft door (21 sq ft) and a 3 ft by 4 ft window (12 sq ft) and the paintable wall area is 399 sq ft. The ceiling is the floor area, 12 x 15 = 180 sq ft. How much paint that needs depends on the product's coverage figure on its label and on the number of coats, so check the can rather than assuming a number.

items: Using the slanted side of a parallelogram or trapezoid as the height. The height is measured at 90 degrees to the parallel sides: using 10 ft instead of 8 ft in the parallelogram example overstates the area by 25% (120 vs 96 sq ft).
Mixing up radius and diameter in a circle. A 10 ft wide circle has a 5 ft radius. Doubling the radius quadruples the area.
Forgetting that curved and angled areas are estimates of the finished layout; flooring is cut to the actual outline, so measure the real edge.
Using square footage of the whole plan when part of it will not receive the finish, such as built-in cabinets or a stair opening. Subtract it.
Combining units. Convert everything to feet or everything to meters before multiplying.
Treating a calculator result as a purchase quantity. Waste, pattern matching and package sizes are separate decisions for your supplier or installer.

sections.text: Check measurements twice and record them on a sketch. If the area feeds structural, electrical or permit work, confirm the figures with your contractor and local building codes.
